item.title: How to Run a Presidential Bid: Ex-Biden Chief Will Gather Aides of 2028 Hopefuls
item.description:
The strategist who led former President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s last two presidential campaigns is organizing a gathering of top aides to several Democrats who are likely to begin running for the White House next year.

The event, set for next month in New York, is being funded in part by the liberal megadonor Alex Soros. It was pitched to the prospective campaign chiefs as a rolling conversation about how to build and maintain the infrastructure for a national political operation.

The private gathering, which was described by nine people briefed on the preparations who spoke on the condition of anonymity, is intended to be far smaller and more private than the 3,000-person convention that Democrats held last week in Denver. It is being convened by Jen O’Malley Dillon, who was the campaign manager for Mr. Biden’s 2020 bid and became the top official overseeing the 2024 campaign for Mr. Biden and then for Vice President Kamala Harris.

The planned event — an unusual gathering in the lead-up to a presidential campaign — shows how Democrats are quietly accelerating their preparations for the 2028 race now that the midterm elections are over.

It is intended to be less a briefing about political strategy or the optimal policy for candidates and more a discussion of the tactics, technology and leadership required for a presidential campaign, the people briefed on the event said. Ms. O’Malley Dillon declined to comment. Mr. Soros could not be reached for comment.

Officials who were invited stressed that the meeting, expected to take place in mid-December, was to be kept secret. One compared it to “Fight Club” — the first rule is do not discuss it — and another said they had been told its existence would not leak to the press.

The invitees included aides for at least eight potential presidential candidates: Ms. Harris, Gov. Andy Beshear of Kentucky, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Senator Mark Kelly of Arizona, Gov. Wes Moore of Maryland, Gov. Gavin Newsom of California, Gov. JB Pritzker of Illinois and Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania. Aides for other possible candidates may still be invited later, and other Democratic operatives who are not affiliated with specific politicians are expected to be included as well.

The invitations offer an early indication of whom Democratic presidential candidates might choose to be their top campaign aides once they formalize their White House ambitions.

Those invited include: Eric Hyers, a longtime Beshear aide; Emma Brown, who is expected to lead Mr. Kelly’s campaign if he runs, and Jen Cox, Mr. Kelly’s chief of staff; Brian Fallon, an aide to Ms. Harris; Quentin Fulks, an aide to Mr. Pritzker who has also worked for Senator Raphael Warnock of Georgia; Michael Halle, who works for Mr. Buttigieg; and Tim Persico and Dana Fritz, who are expected to help lead Mr. Shapiro’s presidential campaign if he runs.

None of the potential candidates are expected to formally announce a campaign this year, but many of them are laying the groundwork.

On Thursday, former aides to Mr. Buttigieg began a group called Team Pete PAC to encourage him to run for president. Ms. Brown has taken a leave of absence from Giffords, the gun safety group Mr. Kelly founded with his wife, former Representative Gabrielle Giffords, to return to Mr. Kelly’s political orbit before he makes a decision on 2028. A group of progressives created a group called Ready for AOC to urge Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Democrat of New York, to run for president.

Some people have said the meeting could be awkward, with officials from rival campaigns-in-waiting gathering to discuss best practices ahead of what is expected to be a crowded and expensive Democratic primary race.

item.title: Agriculture Secretary’s Christian Messages to Staff Went ‘Too Far,’ Judge Says
item.description:
A federal court in California reprimanded Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins on Thursday for Christian religious messages that she had sent to department employees, ruling that they amounted to a violation of the Constitution.

Pointing to the First Amendment’s prohibition on laws “respecting an establishment of religion,” Judge Trina L. Thompson of the U.S. District Court in Northern California limited how Ms. Rollins could promote her religious beliefs in her official duties.

Judge Thompson wrote in a 21-page ruling that “the secretary must recognize certain boundaries when communicating religious messages.” The order said that she must stop “if a colleague asks,” that she could not “create a hostile work environment through persistent unwelcome advances” and that she could not “use official authority to pressure subordinates.”

The judge wrote that Ms. Rollins had gone “too far” when she sent two emails celebrating Christmas and Easter in an explicitly religious manner. In the Christmas email, Ms. Rollins wrote of “our savior Jesus Christ, who came to free us from our sins and open the door to eternal life.” For Easter, Ms. Rollins declared that “he is risen indeed!” and wrote that it was “the greatest story ever told, the foundation of our faith and the abiding hope of all mankind.”

“From the foot of the cross on Good Friday to the stone rolled away from the now empty tomb, sin has been destroyed,” she continued. “Jesus has been raised from the dead. And God has granted each of us victory and new life. And where there is life — risen life — there is hope.”

Judge Thompson, who was appointed by President Joseph R. Biden Jr., stressed that Ms. Rollins was free to express her religious beliefs to “interested colleagues” and in “appropriate conversations.” She added that she was “keenly aware of the sensitivities present in this action,” and that “this court expresses no view whatsoever on what the secretary can and cannot do in her personal capacity.”

But the judge said Ms. Rollins’s messages, sent through official emails to all department employees, appeared “to exploit her position of authority to convey a religious message beyond mere holiday wishes and amounting to coercion.”

“Social pressure alone is not state coercion,” Judge Thompson wrote. But, she added, “the totality of the circumstances here demonstrates such immense pressure to amount to coercion.”

Politico reported on the Easter message earlier this year, and the National Federation of Federal Employees, Americans United for Separation of Church and State and seven department workers sued, saying that Ms. Rollins had “adopted a practice of sending increasingly proselytizing communications.”

In a statement, the plaintiffs and their lawyers praised the ruling.

“Federal employees are public servants, not an audience for their bosses’ personal religious beliefs,” said Randy Erwin, the president of the National Federation of Federal Employees. Rachel Laser, the head of Americans United, said the decision “should send a message to the Trump administration that it cannot misuse taxpayer resources to preach” to federal employees.

The Agriculture Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

item.title: Me, MAGA? Elon Musk Backs Away From a Presidency He Shaped
item.description:
Elon Musk has done a lot for President Trump in the past couple of years.

He spent a cool $290 million to elect him in 2024. He became the wealthiest unelected White House adviser the country had ever known. He spent close to $500 million to help Trump’s allies in the midterms.

Now, though, Musk has a message for the nation: He is not MAGA after all.

That comment came during an interview with my colleague Andrew Ross Sorkin at the DealBook conference yesterday, and I’d encourage you to watch the whole thing. Musk made himself the latest right-leaning cultural figure to distance himself from Trump, following the likes of Joe Rogan and Ben Shapiro.

“I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it,” Musk said, before trying to downplay his political involvement. “I didn’t put a lot of personal attention into it because I focused on, on building SpaceX, Tesla, you know.”

The intense focus on Musk’s spending obscures an important political point. He was never just a donor on the sidelines, nor a mere MAGA adherent (or “dark gothic MAGA,” as he memorably put it). In the opening months of last year, he was the most visible member of the Trump administration besides the president himself — and Musk’s polarizing and chaotic tenure leading the so-called Department of Government Efficiency became a political liability that the administration struggled to shake.

In other words: It’s not just that Musk failed to help Trump win. It’s that in some ways, he could be part of why Trump’s party lost.

Musk was omnipresent in Washington. His aides gutted government agencies like the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and U.S.A.I.D. He was in the Oval Office with his child on his shoulders; wielding a chain saw onstage at the Conservative Political Action Conference; sitting shotgun in a Tesla with Trump on the White House driveway and — perhaps most controversially — at the Defense Department, meeting with Pete Hegseth.

Polls showed that DOGE was unpopular, as was Musk himself. Even people who voted for Trump weren’t quite sure this was what they had signed up for.

“It was sold to the American people in such a way that, ‘This is going to be good for you,’” Jerry Jacob, a tech worker from New Jersey, told me this fall. He voted for Trump in 2024, but he said he found DOGE off-putting. “Are things better now than before? Honestly, I wouldn’t be able to say yes.”

Democrats seized on the image of Trump cozying up to Musk as they built a caricature of a president beholden to the billionaire class and made it core to their midterm pitch. Musk remained a political target long after he departed the White House in the late spring of 2025. His big spending on behalf of Ken Paxton, the Trump ally and Republican Senate nominee in Texas, gave Democrats a new opening to go after their favorite foil.

“Ken Paxton is funded by one dude,” James Talarico, Paxton’s Democratic opponent, said in the closing days of the campaign. “Elon Musk wants our land. He wants our water. He wants our tax dollars. He wants his very own personal United States senator. He is trying to buy Texas.”

“On Nov. 3, we are going to deliver a crystal clear message to the world’s first trillionaire: Texas is not for sale,” Talarico said. He won convincingly.

Now that the political winds have shifted, Musk has, too. He described himself at DealBook as “ideologically quite moderate,” and praised Texas’ newly elected Democratic governor, Gina Hinojosa, as “quite moderate” herself.

It was part of his time-honored ritual of cozying up to the powerful, whoever that is. He has showered right-wing leaders in Argentina, India and Brazil with compliments. He took President Barack Obama on a tour of SpaceX in 2010 and said he voted for Hillary Clinton in 2016 before his expensive mission to elect Trump in 2024.

“You know,” he told Andrew, “American elections are not just about money.”

Hannah Fidelman contributed reporting.

item.title: Top White House Cybersecurity Official Steps Down
item.description:
Sean Cairncross, the top cybersecurity official at the White House, is stepping down from his post and leaving the administration, the White House said in a statement on Thursday.

The departure comes as a series of technological outages have plagued major U.S. companies and federal agencies in recent days.

Mr. Cairncross had been the national cyber director, who helps draft the nation’s cyber strategy and coordinates among agencies on cybersecurity, since August 2025. The circumstances of his departure were not immediately clear.

In the past week, technological problems have slowed banking transactions, disrupted email services, shut down a key system at the National Security Agency and temporarily grounded all commercial air traffic in the United States. Officials have said that those episodes were not caused by malicious cyberattacks. But the lack of a clear explanation for some of the outages has contributed to rising public concern.

President Trump has downplayed the outages as minor incidents caused by routine upgrades, asserting that they were “individual events” unrelated to one another.

“It’s life,” Mr. Trump said while traveling in Manila earlier this week. “When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.”Axios earlier reported news of Mr. Craincross’s departure.

As the Trump administration sought to quell rising public worry about the disruptions, Mr. Cairncross did not make public appearances.

Earlier this year, he played a major role in internal administration deliberations related to artificial intelligence safety risks. But he appeared to be increasingly sidelined from those conversations, especially after Mr. Trump in October tapped the director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, as the A.I. czar.

Mr. Cairncross was seen by colleagues as close to the former White House chief of staff, Susie Wiles. His office has had a high rate of turnover in recent months, according to former officials. The national cybersecurity director, a position created by Congress, has only indirect authority over A.I. issues.

item.title: Technology Promised Ease. Now It’s Making Many Americans Uneasy.
item.description:
The primary benefit of information technology, Steve Ballmer, the former Microsoft chief executive, said in a speech 20 years ago, “is that it empowers people to do what they want to do.”

For decades, this all-American promise seemed borne out, as rapid advances in technology enabled people to create, communicate and consume with an ease that would have once been unimaginable.

But at some point on the path of inexorable progress, the promise seems to have curdled for a large swath of the population. Rather than feeling empowered by the digital tools they have come to rely on, many are now questioning how powerless they may have actually become.

A seven-day stretch that began last week with a global Microsoft outage affecting email and video calls continued with a succession of tech meltdowns, including the grounding of thousands of flights because of problems with outdated air traffic communications equipment. It was capped by the $2 trillion dollar stock market debut of the artificial intelligence company Anthropic, which rocketed an elite few into a new stratosphere of wealth.

Anger had already been building. Well before the series of outages, communities across the country had been pressing for bans on data centers and Flock surveillance cameras, or passing pre-emptive prohibitions on certain kinds of technology, like delivery drones. Schools have banished social media and cellphones, and are facing off with Google over the company’s insistence that classrooms allow A.I.-related products. And the astronomic wealth of tech titans has triggered a ferocious populist reaction, one that partly powered the biggest electoral backlash in generations this month.

And yet the colossal disruptions of this past week have forced people to reckon with how utterly dependent they have become on worldwide computer networks, even before the prospect of the complete A.I. takeover that Silicon Valley power brokers insist is imminent.

As with the period leading up to New Year’s Eve 1999, when experts warned of a potential catastrophic Y2K computing meltdown, Americans in recent days could do little but hope that tech professionals were on top of the problems that could have upended their lives. But even as technology has become far more omnipresent, the techno-optimism at the turn of the new millennium has long faded.

“With Y2K there was this fear that computers are going to become broken,” said Zachary Loeb, a historian of technological disaster at Purdue University who is working on a book on the Y2K scare. “I think in the present there is more of a sense that computers have broken everything.”

The backlash has swelled even as fast-evolving computer technology brings promise along with peril.

Some of the recent outages were triggered when new A.I. tools discovered vulnerabilities and companies rushed to patch them, valuable fixes that brought chaotic side effects. A.I. is making potentially life-changing advances in cancer treatment, while some leading A.I. engineers speak fatalistically of the impending prospect of worldwide unemployment. This week, as fears over computer failures prompted some to start disaster-prepping, others flocked online to try out the blockbuster cultural product of the fall, the video game Grand Theft Auto IV.

As Rabbi Elliott Tepperman sees it, what may have at one point been an intentional bargain — people ceding some control over their daily tasks in return for opportunity and convenience — has become a trap.

“I think we’re way past that bargain,” said Rabbi Tepperman, who in his 2025 Yom Kippur sermon at Bnai Keshet, a synagogue in Montclair, N.J., smashed a smartphone with a hammer. “We’re either addicted or mindlessly giving away our attention for hardly any convenience at all.”

Sixty-nine percent of Americans feel overwhelmed by the number of passwords they have to keep track of, according to the Pew Research Center. Workers at some Fortune 500 companies spend roughly four hours a week — or 5 working weeks a year — toggling between tabs and applications and then having to refocus the brain, according to a 2022 analysis in the Harvard Business Review.

When the trade-off of control for convenience falls short, the problem is more than mere inconvenience. It may be easier to handle personal banking without having to deposit a paycheck at the local branch, but when the bank’s online services fail, the customer discovers that he or she is all but helpless.

“Now that those things are in some ways not working as we’re used to, then we realize how much our agency has sort of been surrendered,” said Bishop Daniel E. Flores of Brownsville, Texas., who was in Baltimore this week for an annual meeting of Catholic bishops, where everyone had to take an early lunch because the digital voting system crashed. “It’s a wake-up moment to re-evaluate how much we — how much do I — want to be dependent.”

Often, the opposition is not to tech itself, but to the sense that it is being foisted on people and communities. In hearing rooms and high school cafeterias around the country, local residents have made the same vociferous objections to data center projects: They are being built not for them, but in the interest of faraway corporations.

“New technology is great,” said Whittney Wood, a D.J. and single mother in central Ohio who narrowly lost a race for state legislature this year in a campaign powered in part by the furious resistance to a local data center. “What I firmly stand against is the big tech people that are shoving these things down our throats, just to make sure that they can get as much profit as possible.”

The sense of futility that runs through these hearings is in some ways belied by the outcomes. Data centers have been successfully blocked in county after county. More than 20 states have introduced or passed bills restricting social media usage among children, though some of these have been challenged in court. And multiple candidates in this year’s midterm elections ran explicitly on platforms of resistance to the power and wealth of big tech — and won.

“A lot of people are feeling like A.I. is just happening to them, and that decisions about this are being made by a fairly small circle of people — and they are responding,” said Kim Daniels, director of the Initiative on Catholic Social Thought and Public Life at Georgetown University. “Workers and families and communities need a much bigger place in the conversation.”

In Silicon Valley, there is a growing awareness of the backlash. Technology leaders are offering defenses of their products, even as their companies are defining the new American economy.

Anthropic’s initial public offering prospectus makes the case that artificial intelligence can positively transform society, from potentially curing cancer to already “helping to shorten the lines at the DMV.” It argues that people who buy Anthropic stock should see themselves as “part of something greater,” not simply as making a “transactional” purchase.

Yet there is broad talk in A.I. circles of the “gradual disempowerment of humans,” said Ruxandra Teslo, a science writer who recently posted a much-discussed essay about “handoverism,” the idea circulating in Silicon Valley that humanity should — or will soon be forced to — cede control of civilization to a benevolent A.I.

“For the first time in Silicon Valley, increasing human agency doesn’t seem to even be the stated goal,” she said.

Not everyone in the tech world is enthusiastic about this, she said, but many are resigned to it. The way some discuss the scenario suggests that they, too, feel powerless, unable to curb the development of a technology that they believe is leading in a very grim direction.

“I’ve seen some people even welcome the fact that there is a backlash,” Ms. Teslo said. “They want someone to stop them from making these systems. Because they feel like they cannot stop themselves.”

Yair Rosenberg contributed reporting.

item.title: California Thieves Carried Out String of Train Heists, Prosecutors Say
item.description:
The train robberies outlined in the 49-page indictment read like a Hollywood treatment for a Wild West-meets-the-A.I.-age heist movie.

Over more than two years, prosecutors say, a crew of 14 people carried out a series of freight train heists in Southern California, boarding the slow-moving trains in early-morning darkness. After sawing their way into boxcars stuffed with sneakers and electronics, they forced the trains to a stop, filled waiting getaway vans with the goods and fled to stash houses, according to the grand jury indictment unsealed on Thursday.

The thieves were as meticulous in documenting their exploits as they were in planning them, according to the indictment, which includes images from a video showing one of the accused using a circular saw to cut the lock of a train car, sparks flying. In some instances, those charged had posted videos of their crimes to social media, officials said.

The group called themselves the “Los Trenes” — Spanish for “The Trains,” according to prosecutors. In an Instagram chat described in the indictment, the crew members shared A.I.-generated images of black-clad men in black BMWs driving alongside a train as their accomplices unload boxes of Nike shoes.

Over more than two years, prosecutors say, their take was staggering: more than $22 million worth of Nike, Hoka and Crocs shoes, as well as electronics and power tools. Altogether, the crew plundered more than three dozen train cars, officials said.

Law enforcement officers on Thursday fanned out across Southern California to make arrests.

The charges followed a 14-month task force investigation, named Operation CoolKicks, that involved numerous agencies, including the Los Angeles Police Department, the Department of Justice, the Los Angeles District Attorney’s Office, Homeland Security Investigations and the Union Pacific Railroad police.

Jim McDonnell, chief of the Los Angeles Police Department, said at a news conference on Thursday that the indictment “marks the largest property crime bust in L.A.P.D. and railroad history.”

“This is much more than a modern-day train robbery,” he said. “It was a highly coordinated operation that disrupted our nation’s supply chain.”

The indictment charged 14 men with 17 felony counts related to the heists, and they face decades in prison if convicted, according to the Justice Department. It was unclear whether any of the men charged had legal representation.

Southern California is a hub for America’s supply chain, with goods arriving by sea at two ports, Los Angeles and Long Beach, where they are then loaded onto trains bound for warehouses around the country. In recent years, trains, especially in the Los Angeles area, have been targeted by thieves with greater frequency, and law enforcement has devoted more resources to countering the crimes.

“The scale of the theft is staggering,” said Bill Essayli, the first assistant U.S. attorney in Los Angeles, whose office is prosecuting the case. Mr. Essayli posted a video on X of the man prosecutors say was the crew’s ringleader sawing off a lock on a train car.

“I encourage criminals to film themselves while committing crimes,” Mr. Essayli said at the news conference. “It makes our jobs a lot easier.”

The robbery crew had their own network of stash houses and warehouses across the region, according to the indictment. Once the looted goods were safely stored, they arranged to sell the products to buyers who would then resell them to the public. One company, a sneaker reseller identified only as “Company 1” in the indictment, operated a warehouse in Santa Monica, Calif., and paid more than $1 million over the last two years for stolen Nikes, prosecutors say.

The indictment describes a series of train heists from February of 2024 until this summer. The goods had been on their way to places all around the country, including Indiana, Texas, Kansas and Pennsylvania.

Each heist involved several men, with some jumping onboard the moving freight trains, which were as much as three miles long. Other members of the crew, using rented vans and trucks, positioned themselves ahead of the train’s route at an agreed-upon, often remote and isolated, location. Once the train reached that spot, one of the men on board would cut the hose supplying air to the brakes, “forcing the trains to come to an emergency stop,” prosecutors wrote.

Once the getaway vehicles were stuffed with sneakers or tools or electronics, the goods would be stored at stash houses while the men arranged transactions with resellers.

Well before the arrests this week, the crew had hints that law enforcement officers were on their tail.

According to the indictment, an unnamed co-conspirator sent a text to one of the defendants saying he had been arrested for receiving stolen property. He wrote that he “could have easily thru your name under the bus.”

The last robbery detailed in the indictment was on Aug. 6. The man prosecutors say was the leader of the operation boarded a train and discovered an especially valuable stash of unreleased Nike Air Jordan “Space Jam” sneakers.

Prosecutors say he texted a photograph to the group chat. “No way,” one of the members replied. “Sheeeesh,” wrote another.

item.title: Justice Department Gives Up on Alaska Senate Lawsuit
item.description:
The Trump administration is giving up its bid to block the certification of results in Alaska’s Senate race, abandoning a legal maneuver that threatened to prevent Senator-elect Mary Peltola, a Democrat, from taking office.

The Justice Department asked a federal court to declare its lawsuit against Alaska moot on Thursday, two days after The Associated Press called the competitive race for Ms. Peltola.

Democrats helped recruit a second candidate with a name similar to that of the Republican incumbent, Senator Dan S. Sullivan, The New York Times reported. On President Trump’s order, the Justice Department had argued even before Election Day, and before The Times’s report, that Alaska should not certify a narrow victory for Ms. Peltola until it could be determined that her win was not due to voter confusion.

But critics called the move legally meritless, and lawyers for the state of Alaska, where Republicans control the governorship and the Legislature, sought to have the case dismissed.

Ms. Peltola ended up winning by more than four percentage points, a wide enough margin that Mr. Sullivan would still have lost even if every ballot cast for the lesser-known candidate had gone to him.

In a court filing on Thursday, the Justice Department maintained that its initial bid had merit, but it conceded that it would be impossible for its lawyers to interrogate voters about their reasoning now that ballots had been de-identified. Lawyers for the Justice Department “reluctantly” acknowledged that “there no longer exists any means” to figure out whether voters for the potential spoiler, Dan J. Sullivan, meant to pick the incumbent senator instead, and therefore no way to vindicate its claims.

A judge denied the Trump administration’s request to segregate ballots cast for Dan J. Sullivan ahead of the election, but the Justice Department appealed.

The judge could still rule on the merits of the case, even though the Justice Department argues the point is moot.

In October, the Justice Department announced it was investigating Democrats who recruited a decoy Alaska Senate candidate over potential illegal activity. Thursday’s filings did not address the status of that inquiry, which prosecutors acknowledged might never yield criminal charges.

The Justice Department sent letters to 20 Democrats informing them that they might be targets or asking them to preserve their records, and issued hundreds of subpoenas, according to a person familiar with the investigation who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation.

Ms. Peltola has claimed she was unaware of the plan to recruit a spoiler.

Mr. Sullivan’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In a statement responding to Thursday’s filing, Ms. Peltola said that “voters sent a very clear message about the direction they want our state to go in” and added that she was eager to “get to work on behalf of all Alaskans.”

“For Alaskans, there is only one direction: forward,” she said.

Kellen Browning contributed reporting from Anchorage and Devlin Barrett from Washington.
